title: Chapter 4. When being a millionaire gives you no power, because there are no rich or poor

blocks.text: There is a sentence of Pedro's that sounds like a challenge and, read properly, is a description of a different world: “When being a millionaire gives you no power, because there are no rich or poor.” The point is not to hate those who have much, or to point at a person. It is to imagine an arrangement in which fortune no longer commands, because no one lives above anyone else's dignity, or beneath it.

blocks.text: Chapter 1 left us measured in four coins. Chapter 2 dreamed the collapse of that wage, with humanoids working for humans. Chapter 3 proposed enough coupons for what is necessary. This chapter closes the arc: if the necessary is covered and heavy work is not rented out, what would being a millionaire be for? Today it often serves to command. It buys other people's time, doors, decisions, silence, fear. Money, which began as a help for barter, climbed onto the altar and became power. Pedro holds that that power fades when the inequality that feeds it disappears. There are no rich or poor. That is why the millionaire, if the word remained as a fossil, would no longer frighten or give orders.

blocks.text: It is important not to confuse the horizon with the present. Today there are rich and there are poor. Today money gives power, sometimes a great deal, sometimes quietly, almost always more than is admitted. This book will not pretend otherwise, nor will it design an enemy with a first name and a surname. It will say, calmly, that this is not a fate. It is a habit. Habits can be left behind.

blocks.text: “There are no rich or poor” does not mean that everyone is identical, or that craft, talent, taste or difference disappear. It means that those differences are no longer translated into a life that is bought and a life that is sold. One person may know more about a garden, another about music, another about mending, another about care. No one, by having a higher number in an account, will be able to dispose of other people's day, or of the lagoon, or of the common decision. The millionaire ceases to be a figure of power when the million opens no door that is closed to the rest. If the doors are open in another way — by the coupon, by the machine that works, by what belongs to everyone — the million remains an ornament, or evaporates.

blocks.text: That is a moral idea before it is an accounting idea. Money measured us: as much as you have, so much are you worth. If that rod is taken away, a person is measured again by what they do, by what they care for, by what they keep, by how they are in a dealing. Chapter 6 will say that, without the struggle for economic power, professional politics loses its fuel. Here is the root: the power to command is fed by some being able to buy what is denied to others. Cut that difference, and command deflates.

blocks.text: These pages do not ask for a scene of dispossession or a revenge. They ask for a change of axis. The abundance of the machines, if it is shared, and the right to what is necessary, if it is guaranteed, make accumulation less necessary as a shield and as a weapon. Anyone who wants to accumulate memories, crafts, friends, hours on the shore may do so. What would no longer be accumulated is the right to command another person's life. Being a millionaire, in that world, would give you no power because power would no longer be for sale.

blocks.text: Some will smile and say that there will always be those who want more, and those who take advantage, and those who invent a new hierarchy. It is possible. Human beings do not become angels because hunger is taken from them. This chapter does not promise holiness. It promises, if anything, to take from profit its thickest lever. Anyone who wants to command would have to persuade, not buy. Anyone who wants to stand out would have to stand out by what they contribute, not by what they prevent. Not all conflicts would disappear — Pedro will say so later, and the nuance matters — but many of those that today are, at bottom, a business would come to an end.

blocks.text: Some will ask how one arrives there without breaking everything. The book does not offer a decree. It offers a sequence: that the machines work for us, not for an owner; that each person has what is necessary; that, then, fortune ceases to be a throne. The order of the chapters is the order of the idea. First the wage as the only passport falls away. Then the table is covered. Then the million no longer commands. If the order is reversed, if equality is proclaimed and bread is left in the hands of whoever owns the machine, a pretty word will have been said and something else will have been done.

blocks.text: In Cartagena there are old coins that no longer buy a loaf and, even so, still speak of those who minted them and those who sweated for them. The metal lasted longer than the power of many. It is a humble lesson for this chapter: the power of money is historical, not natural. It was born when work was priced. It can end when work ceases to be priced and the necessary ceases to be a privilege. The coins in the museum command no one. One day, today's accounts could come to resemble those pieces: objects of a time when being a millionaire still gave power.

blocks.text: From the Mar Menor, the idea can be said without figures. The lagoon does not belong to whoever has the most. Neither does the sunset. A society in which there are no rich or poor is not a society without beauty or difference: it is a society in which beauty and difference cannot be bought in order to exclude. The water remains water. The person, a person. And the millionaire, if the word remains, a memory of when money measured us and governed us with the same rule.

blocks.text: This is the horizon, not the bulletin of the day. It is written so that it will not be confused with a fact, and so that the chapter that follows will not be misread. Because even in a world without rich or poor, even with the table covered, a hole can remain in a life: what to do with time, how not to fill it with comforts that take more than they give. Money, when it leaves the altar, does not by itself fill what it left empty while it stood there. To that hole, and to what may occupy it in another way, the next page is devoted.

blocks.text: While it was the measure of almost everything, money also measured prestige and fear. A high number opened. A low number closed. In the world of this chapter, that compass is broken on purpose. It no longer indicates a person's value, because value has returned to other rods: care, the word that is kept, the craft well done, the shore that is shared. Being a millionaire gives you no power because power, if it remains, is no longer bought. And there are no rich or poor because the necessary has not been left to luck or to lineage. It is a demanding horizon. That is why it is written here in full, and not as if it had already dawned.

blocks.text: Those who are poor today do not need a book to explain to them what it is to go without. Those who have much today do not need, either, to be turned into an enemy. The chapter speaks of an arrangement, not a hunt. If one day there are no rich or poor, it will be because the necessary ceased to be booty and command ceased to be for sale. Until then, Pedro's sentence serves as a compass: a million that opens no doors against others is a million that no longer commands.

blocks.text: In the square, that idea is understood without theorems. No one should be able to buy a neighbour's silence, or the vote of a street, or the fate of a lagoon. If money does not open those doors, being a millionaire is, at most, an anecdote. If it does open them, no equality is worth anything. This chapter keeps to the first of those outcomes, and leaves the second as the world one wants to leave behind.
